title: Organic Chemistry
seo_title: Year 11 Science: Organic Chemistry Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_text: Crude oil, hydrocarbons and alkanes; fractional distillation and petrochemicals; properties of hydrocarbons (boiling point, viscosity, flammability) and complete combustion; cracking and alkenes; the test for alkenes with bromine water.

key_big: Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; alkenes are CₙH₂ₙ.
key_sub: Longer chains: higher boiling point, less flammable.
body_html:
How to think about it

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons separated by boiling point.

  • Alkanes: methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀.
  • Longer chains have higher boiling points, are more viscous and less flammable.
  • Cracking breaks long alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes. Alkenes turn bromine water from orange to colourless.
Example

Formula of an alkane with 5 carbons?

2 × 5 + 2 = 12

Answer: C₅H₁₂

Example

C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + ?

C: 10 − 8 = 2

H: 22 − 18 = 4

Answer: C₂H₄

Common mistakes

  • Thinking longer chains are more flammable.
  • Thinking alkenes are saturated.
  • Thinking bromine water goes colourless with alkanes.

faq.q: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
faq.a: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. For example, propane has 3 carbons and 8 hydrogens: C₃H₈.
Long-chain hydrocarbons are heated (with a catalyst or steam) and break into shorter alkanes and alkenes.

faq.q: How do you test for an alkene?
faq.a: Shake it with bromine water. An alkene turns it from orange to colourless; an alkane leaves it orange.
